scope: Selected Hebrew Bible narratives, people, historical regions and political entities. This is not a complete canonical index, a settled biblical chronology, a GIS map or an independent historical certification.
sourcePolicy: Scripture references support what the biblical books narrate. Museum records and academic historical commentary are separately attributed to their narrower claims. Royal monuments can be partisan political sources. Do not infer a person, event or modern community identity from an ancient imperial label alone.

sennacherib-prism.title: Israel Museum - The Assyrian campaign in Judah as told by the Sennacherib Prism
sennacherib-prism.scope: Assyrian royal inscription on 701 BCE Judah campaign, tribute and royal claims; does not verify the Bible's explanation of Jerusalem's outcome.

lachish-relief.title: British Museum - Sennacherib's Lachish assault relief
lachish-relief.scope: Material evidence of Assyrian depiction of Lachish campaign; royal propaganda and historical reconstruction require interpretation.

black-obelisk.title: British Museum - Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
black-obelisk.scope: Neo-Assyrian royal monument naming tribute of Jehu of the House of Omri; does not independently recount his coup.

cyrus-cylinder.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art - Cyrus and the Judean Diaspora
cyrus-cylinder.scope: The Cyrus Cylinder describes Babylonian imperial religious policy, not a specific decree naming Jews or Jerusalem.

babylon-cylinder.title: British Museum - Nebuchadnezzar II building inscription
babylon-cylinder.scope: Inscribed evidence of Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylonian building projects, not proof of specific biblical court stories.

people.name: Abraham
people.disambiguation: Patriarch in Genesis, distinct from later namesakes.
people.summary: Genesis narrates Abram's call and the covenant promises, including his renaming as Abraham.

people.name: Sarah
people.disambiguation: Wife of Abraham in Genesis.
people.summary: Genesis describes Sarai's renaming as Sarah and the promised birth of Isaac.

people.name: Isaac
people.disambiguation: Son of Abraham and Sarah, not Ishmael.
people.summary: Genesis portrays Isaac in the ancestral narratives and identifies Jacob and Esau as his sons.

people.name: Jacob, called Israel
people.disambiguation: The patriarch called Israel, not the later northern kingdom bearing that name.
people.summary: Genesis narrates Jacob's renaming as Israel and the family whose descendants figure in the tribal narratives.

people.name: Joseph son of Jacob
people.disambiguation: The Joseph of Genesis, distinct from Joseph of Nazareth.
people.summary: Genesis portrays Joseph's rise in Egypt and eventual reconciliation with his brothers.

people.name: Moses
people.disambiguation: The leader in Exodus and Deuteronomy, not an alternative name for another prophet.
people.summary: Exodus presents Moses as the leader of Israel's departure from Egypt and mediator of the Sinai covenant.

people.name: Aaron
people.disambiguation: Brother of Moses and Miriam, distinct from later priestly figures.
people.summary: Exodus and Numbers identify Aaron in the departure narratives and priestly traditions.

people.name: Miriam
people.disambiguation: Sister of Moses and Aaron, distinct from later women named Mary.
people.summary: Exodus calls Miriam a prophet and describes her song after the crossing.

people.name: Joshua son of Nun
people.disambiguation: Israelite leader in Joshua, not another biblical Joshua or Jesus.
people.summary: Joshua reports the crossing of the Jordan and the Israelites' entry into the land.

people.name: Deborah the judge
people.disambiguation: Prophet and judge in Judges 4-5, not Rebekah's nurse in Genesis.
people.summary: Judges depicts Deborah judging Israel and participating in the narrative of Barak's campaign.

people.name: Ruth
people.disambiguation: The Moabite woman in Ruth, distinct from any later namesakes.
people.summary: The book of Ruth recounts her loyalty to Naomi and her marriage to Boaz.

people.name: Samuel
people.disambiguation: Prophet and judge associated with Shiloh, distinct from King Saul.
people.summary: First Samuel recounts Samuel's call and his role in the transition to kingship.

people.name: Saul king of Israel
people.disambiguation: The first monarch in 1 Samuel, not Saul of Tarsus in Acts.
people.summary: First Samuel depicts Saul's anointing as king and conflict with David.

people.name: David
people.disambiguation: The Judahite king in Samuel and Kings, distinct from later descendants bearing his name.
people.summary: Second Samuel narrates David's enthronement and the establishment of Jerusalem as his capital.

people.name: Solomon
people.disambiguation: David's son and successor as king, not a stand-in for every royal wisdom author.
people.summary: First Kings describes Solomon's reign and the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem.

people.name: Rehoboam
people.disambiguation: King of Judah after the kingdom division, not Jeroboam.
people.summary: First Kings recounts Rehoboam's response to the tribes' petition and the division of royal rule.

people.name: Jeroboam son of Nebat
people.disambiguation: Founder of the northern kingdom's royal line, distinct from Jeroboam II.
people.summary: First Kings presents Jeroboam's kingship after the division and the rival cult sites at Bethel and Dan.

people.name: Ahab king of Israel
people.disambiguation: Ninth-century northern king, not a Judahite ruler.
people.summary: First Kings describes Ahab's rule and Elijah's confrontation with the prophets of Baal.

people.name: Elijah
people.disambiguation: Prophet active in First and Second Kings.
people.summary: The Elijah narratives include the Carmel confrontation and the episode of his departure.

people.name: Elisha
people.disambiguation: Prophet succeeding Elijah, not the similarly sounding name Elijah.
people.summary: Second Kings describes Elisha's ministry following Elijah's departure.

people.name: Jehu king of Israel
people.disambiguation: King whose coup is narrated in 2 Kings 9-10, distinct from Jehu son of Hanani.
people.summary: Second Kings recounts Jehu's violent succession. An Assyrian obelisk separately attests tribute associated with a Jehu of the House of Omri, not the biblical coup's details.

people.name: Jeroboam son of Joash
people.disambiguation: Later king of northern Israel, distinct from Jeroboam son of Nebat.
people.summary: Second Kings narrates his reign; Amos is dated by its superscription to his period.

people.name: Amos
people.disambiguation: Prophetic voice in the book bearing his name.
people.summary: Amos' superscription places his prophetic activity in the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel.

people.name: Hosea the prophet
people.disambiguation: The prophet, not King Hoshea of Israel.
people.summary: Hosea is introduced as a prophetic voice across northern Israel's late monarchy.

people.name: Isaiah son of Amoz
people.disambiguation: The prophet named in Isaiah 1:1, not a claim about single authorship of every chapter of Isaiah.
people.summary: Isaiah's superscription places the prophetic book in the era of several kings of Judah. The book contains narratives connected with Hezekiah and Assyria.

people.name: Micah of Moresheth
people.disambiguation: Prophet in the book bearing his name, not the Micah in Judges 17.
people.summary: Micah's superscription locates his oracles in the periods of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.

people.name: Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria
people.disambiguation: Assyrian ruler named in 2 Kings, distinct from Sennacherib and Shalmaneser.
people.summary: Second Kings reports Assyrian incursions and deportations under Tiglath-pileser.

people.name: Shalmaneser king of Assyria
people.disambiguation: The Assyrian king in 2 Kings 17, not Shalmaneser III of the Black Obelisk.
people.summary: Second Kings records Hoshea's submission and subsequent conflict with Shalmaneser. Attribution of all subsequent siege activity is a separate historical question.

people.name: Hoshea son of Elah
people.disambiguation: Last ruler of northern Israel named in 2 Kings, not the prophet Hosea.
people.summary: Second Kings identifies Hoshea as Israel's king during the Assyrian campaigns preceding Samaria's fall.

people.name: Hezekiah king of Judah
people.disambiguation: Judahite king in the Assyrian campaign narratives, not a king of northern Israel.
people.summary: Second Kings recounts Hezekiah's reforms, his tribute and Jerusalem's crisis during Sennacherib's campaign.

people.name: Sennacherib king of Assyria
people.disambiguation: Neo-Assyrian monarch, distinct from Shalmaneser and Tiglath-pileser.
people.summary: Second Kings and Isaiah record Sennacherib's campaign against Judah. Contemporary Assyrian royal sources describe his successes and Hezekiah's tribute, with different emphases from the biblical narrative.

people.name: Jonah son of Amittai
people.disambiguation: Prophet named in 2 Kings and in the narrative book of Jonah.
people.summary: The book of Jonah narrates a prophetic mission to Nineveh. The narrative's literary and historical questions should not be settled by the location entry alone.

people.name: Nahum of Elkosh
people.disambiguation: Prophet to whom the book of Nahum is attributed, not a named Assyrian court chronicler.
people.summary: Nahum contains an oracle concerning Nineveh. Its rhetoric cannot by itself be used as an archaeological account of the city's capture.

people.name: Josiah king of Judah
people.disambiguation: Judahite king associated with the discovery of a scroll and covenant reform.
people.summary: Second Kings presents Josiah's temple reforms and the public renewal of the covenant.

people.name: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah
people.disambiguation: Prophet in the book of Jeremiah, not King Josiah's high priest.
people.summary: Jeremiah's book places his ministry across the last decades of Judah's kingdom and the Jerusalem catastrophe.

people.name: Zedekiah king of Judah
people.disambiguation: Last reigning king of Judah in the 2 Kings 25 account, distinct from other biblical Zedekiahs.
people.summary: Second Kings narrates Zedekiah's rebellion, the siege and the destruction of Jerusalem.

people.name: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
people.disambiguation: Neo-Babylonian king in Kings and Daniel, not his father Nabopolassar.
people.summary: Second Kings and Jeremiah identify Nebuchadnezzar with campaigns and deportations involving Judah. Daniel sets court narratives under him.

people.name: Ezekiel son of Buzi
people.disambiguation: Prophet in the exile setting of Ezekiel, not another man sharing the name.
people.summary: The book situates Ezekiel among exiles by the Chebar canal in Babylonia rather than at the city centre of Babylon.

people.name: Daniel
people.disambiguation: The Daniel of the book of Daniel; its literary-historical composition and dates are debated.
people.summary: Daniel's opening chapter locates its court stories in a Babylonian setting. This profile does not present the work as independently verified court documentation.

people.name: Cyrus king of Persia
people.disambiguation: Persian monarch, distinct from any other Cyrus in later historical writing.
people.summary: Ezra and Chronicles attribute an authorisation to Cyrus for a return and rebuilding programme. The Cyrus Cylinder is related imperial evidence but does not mention Jerusalem or Jewish returnees.

people.name: Ezra the scribe
people.disambiguation: Priest and scribe in Ezra-Nehemiah; not the title of every returning leader.
people.summary: Ezra describes a later mission to Jerusalem involving teaching Torah and community reforms.

people.name: Nehemiah
people.disambiguation: Official and wall-building organiser in Nehemiah, distinct from other men named Nehemiah.
people.summary: Nehemiah recounts efforts to repair Jerusalem's defences and to organise public life.

people.name: Esther
people.disambiguation: Queen in the book of Esther; the story's literary and historical setting is not assumed to be independently verified.
people.summary: Esther describes a Jewish woman in the Persian court and a crisis facing the Jewish population.

places.name: Canaan (biblical region)
places.summary: A regional name in the ancestral narratives, without a single fixed boundary applicable to every period.
places.caution: The narrative does not provide a reconstructable journey path or a unique archaeological border.

places.name: Sinai wilderness and mountain
places.summary: Exodus locates the covenant narrative in the wilderness of Sinai.
places.caution: Identification of the mountain and precise campsite is disputed; this is not a mapped coordinate.

places.name: Shiloh
places.summary: Sanctuary setting in the books of Joshua, Judges and 1 Samuel.
places.caution: The site association does not establish a precise spot for Samuel's reported experience.

places.name: Kingdom of Israel (north)
places.summary: A political designation for the northern monarchy in Kings and prophetic superscriptions.
places.caution: Not the patriarch Jacob, not the entire nation at every date, and not a fixed geographical polygon.

places.name: Kingdom of Judah
places.summary: The southern monarchy described in Kings, Chronicles and the prophetic books.
places.caution: The kingdom's changing political control is not represented by a fixed or surveyed outline.

places.name: Mount Carmel (region)
places.summary: Mount named in the prophetic confrontation recorded in 1 Kings.
places.caution: The literary episode does not fix the position of an individual altar or meeting site.

places.name: Samaria (ancient capital)
places.summary: The royal city of the northern kingdom and the subject of the Assyrian capture in Kings.
places.caution: Distinguish the city from the wider region called Samaria in the Gospels and later eras.

places.name: Assyria (imperial polity)
places.summary: A historical imperial power whose rulers appear in the Hebrew Bible's accounts of Israel and Judah.
places.caution: Modern Assyrian identities are not equivalent to the changing borders of an ancient imperial state.

places.name: Nineveh
places.summary: Important Assyrian royal centre and the named setting of Jonah and Nahum.
places.caution: The site is an ancient city; Jonah's conversations and Nahum's prophecy are distinct literary claims.

places.name: Lachish
places.summary: Judean fortified city associated with Sennacherib's campaign in Kings and palace reliefs.
places.caution: Assyrian reliefs glorify victory; the excavated site is not proof of every biblical diplomatic exchange.

places.name: Babylonia (imperial polity)
places.summary: The imperial domain associated with the capture of Jerusalem and Judean exile narratives.
places.caution: The state is not one city, and a narrative located among exiles need not occur within the city of Babylon.

places.name: Babylon (city)
places.summary: The Mesopotamian city at the centre of Neo-Babylonian imperial rule and Daniel's court setting.
places.caution: This entry distinguishes the city from the territory of Babylonia and does not independently verify Daniel's literary episodes.

places.name: Persian Empire (Achaemenid)
places.summary: Empire under Cyrus and later rulers in the Ezra-Nehemiah and Esther narratives.
places.caution: This is a political designation, not an exact route or single point on a map.

places.name: Susa (Shushan)
places.summary: Ancient city named as a Persian court setting in Esther and Nehemiah.
places.caution: Susa as a city is historically attested; that does not independently establish every detail of Esther's literary narrative.

events.title: Call and covenant with Abraham
events.summary: Genesis narrates Abram's departure toward Canaan and a promise concerning his descendants.
events.qualification: Later narrative genealogies belong to the ancestral story, not to an externally established itinerary.

events.title: Israel's departure from Egypt
events.summary: Exodus narrates the departure, Passover and the crossing tradition.
events.qualification: The geography, dating and external historical verification of the Exodus remain disputed.

events.title: Covenant at Sinai
events.summary: Exodus places the giving of covenant teaching at Sinai.
events.qualification: The precise identification of the biblical mountain is disputed.

events.title: Israel crosses the Jordan
events.summary: Joshua narrates the crossing at the start of Israel's entry into the land.
events.qualification: This is the biblical story's sequence; no comprehensive archaeological reconstruction is asserted.

events.title: Ruth and Boaz
events.summary: Ruth recounts the family relationship that the book connects with David's genealogy.
events.qualification: The literary narrative is not an independently dated local case record.

events.title: Samuel and the rise of monarchy
events.summary: First Samuel portrays Samuel's call and the selection of Saul as king.
events.qualification: Shiloh is associated with Samuel's childhood; Saul's anointing is not placed at Shiloh by this entry.

events.title: David's kingship in Jerusalem
events.summary: Second Samuel describes David's accession and Jerusalem becoming his centre.
events.qualification: The biblical kingdom account is not a claim of uncontroversial archaeological borders.

events.title: Dedication of Solomon's temple
events.summary: First Kings narrates the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem.
events.qualification: Architectural details in Scripture do not constitute an excavated plan of the temple.

events.title: Division of royal rule
events.summary: First Kings recounts the division between the kingdoms associated with Rehoboam and Jeroboam.
events.qualification: The kingdom labels are political summaries, not fixed surveyed borders.

events.title: Elijah's confrontation on Carmel
events.summary: First Kings depicts Elijah's confrontation with the prophets of Baal during Ahab's reign.
events.qualification: The mount is named in the text; a pinpoint location for the encounter is not established.

events.title: Jehu's violent accession
events.summary: Second Kings narrates the coup and succession of Jehu.
events.qualification: The Black Obelisk independently attests tribute associated with Jehu, not this narrative's dialogue or executions.

events.title: Reign of Jeroboam II and Amos
events.summary: Second Kings dates a northern reign and Amos' superscription places the prophetic book in the same broad period.
events.qualification: This literary alignment does not establish the date of each individual oracle.

events.title: Hosea's prophetic ministry
events.summary: The opening of Hosea attributes its oracles to the period of northern Israel's late monarchy.
events.qualification: A prophetic superscription is the primary source for the claimed period.

events.title: Assyrian deportations under Tiglath-pileser
events.summary: Second Kings describes territorial conquests and deportations under Tiglath-pileser of Assyria.
events.qualification: Do not collapse multiple campaigns or kings into a single conquest.

events.title: Isaiah and Micah in Judah
events.summary: The prophetic superscriptions situate Isaiah and Micah amid the kingdom of Judah.
events.qualification: The books include later material and differing scholarly views of composition.

events.title: Assyrian conquest of Samaria
events.summary: Second Kings describes Assyrian pressure on Hoshea and the capture of Samaria.
events.qualification: Kings names Shalmaneser in initiating operations; responsibility for the final capture is debated.

events.title: Assyrian campaign against Lachish
events.summary: Second Kings places Assyrian troops at Lachish and reports the crisis confronting Judah.
events.qualification: The Assyrian palace reliefs attest a royal depiction of the siege, not every detail of the Bible's Jerusalem account.

events.title: Jerusalem confronted by Sennacherib
events.summary: Second Kings and Isaiah describe Jerusalem's crisis under Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Assyrian campaign.
events.qualification: The Assyrian prism boasts of Hezekiah's confinement and tribute. It does not claim Jerusalem was captured, and neither royal source independently settles the biblical miracle claim.

events.title: Jonah's mission in the Nineveh narrative
events.summary: Jonah portrays a prophet calling the people of Nineveh to repentance.
events.qualification: The story is indexed as a biblical narrative, not independently verified Ninevite civic history.

events.title: Nahum's oracle concerning Nineveh
events.summary: Nahum speaks rhetorically of judgment against Nineveh.
events.qualification: The text is prophetic literature, not a stand-alone excavation report of the city's destruction.

events.title: Josiah's covenant reform
events.summary: Second Kings narrates the discovery of a scroll and covenant renewal.
events.qualification: The account is a biblical presentation of reform; historical assessment requires separate sources.

events.title: Fall of Jerusalem and deportations
events.summary: Second Kings recounts the siege, destruction of Jerusalem and the removal of the Judahite monarchy.
events.qualification: The historical capture and individual literary details require distinction; the event is not assigned invented exact coordinates.

events.title: Life and literature of the Babylonian exile
events.summary: Ezekiel begins among exiles by the Chebar canal; Daniel narrates court stories in Babylon.
events.qualification: Ezekiel's canal setting is not the exact location of Babylon city; Daniel's court narrative has literary-historical debates.

events.title: Cyrus and the return tradition
events.summary: Ezra attributes a return and temple-rebuilding authorisation to Cyrus.
events.qualification: The Cyrus Cylinder describes broad imperial policies but does not itself mention Jewish exiles or Jerusalem. Ezra's later mission is not dated to Cyrus' initial decree.

events.title: Nehemiah and Jerusalem's walls
events.summary: Nehemiah records a programme to repair Jerusalem's walls and reorganise the community.
events.qualification: Ezra and Nehemiah are linked through literary setting, not necessarily attendance at every episode.

events.title: Esther's story in the Persian court
events.summary: Esther narrates a crisis involving the Jewish community at the court in Susa.
events.qualification: The literary-historical status of Esther's court narrative is debated; the name Susa is not contested as an ancient city.
